question.prompt: What is the maximum number of points of intersection of the graphs of two different fourth degree polynomial functions \(y = p(x)\) and \(y = q(x),\) each with leading coefficient \(1?\)

solutions.explanation:
An intersection occurs exactly when \(p(x)=q(x)\), so consider the zeros of
\[
h(x)=p(x)-q(x).
\]
Both polynomials have leading term \(x^4\), which cancels in the subtraction. Thus \(h\) has degree at most \(3\). It is not the zero polynomial, because the two polynomial functions are different.

A nonzero polynomial of degree at most \(3\) has at most three distinct real zeros. To see why, the factor theorem says that a zero \(r\) supplies a factor \(x-r\). Distinct zeros successively supply distinct linear factors, so four distinct zeros would require degree at least \(4\). Each zero of \(h\) gives exactly one intersection point, so there are at most three intersections.

This bound is attainable. Take
\[
p(x)=x^4,\qquad q(x)=x^4+x(x-1)(x+1).
\]
These are different fourth-degree polynomials with leading coefficient \(1\). Their values agree exactly when \(x(x-1)(x+1)=0\), namely at \(x=-1,0,1\). Hence their graphs have three distinct intersections. The maximum is \(3\), choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
solutions.title: Subtract the polynomials and attain the root bound
